Real Estate Future Forum · What I experienced and the questions I took away.

  • I attended day three of the Real Estate Future Forum in Riyadh in 2026. The discussion moved beyond buildings and skylines towards how people live in cities, how communities form, and how a place gains meaning. I left thinking more about the human purpose of development than the visible scale of a project.
  • In my reflection, I referred to a point made by Peter Jonathan Jameson about the importance of people, proximity, and interaction. I also described Sir Richard Branson’s emphasis on culture, experience, and the people within a business.
  • For my current interests, the forum offers a reminder to ask who a project is intended to serve. Investment and development can be discussed through numbers and physical outputs, but the experience of people is another part of the picture I want to understand.
  • This event sits alongside finance, technology, and governance experiences in my portfolio. Together, they encourage me to look beyond the most visible element of a subject and consider the wider organisation and purpose around it.
01 / 04

A human perspective on development

I attended day three of the Real Estate Future Forum in Riyadh in 2026.

The discussion moved beyond buildings and skylines towards how people live in cities, how communities form, and how a place gains meaning. I left thinking more about the human purpose of development than the visible scale of a project.

The connection

The themes I noticed included sustainability, density, lifestyle, and human-centred planning.

Read the deeper context+

What stayed with me was the idea that a physical development needs a social purpose. The experience broadened the way I thought about business and investment.

02 / 04

Ideas from the discussions

In my reflection, I referred to a point made by Peter Jonathan Jameson about the importance of people, proximity, and interaction.

I also described Sir Richard Branson’s emphasis on culture, experience, and the people within a business.

The connection

Hearing those ideas as an attendee made me reconsider the most obvious way to look at a development.

Read the deeper context+

A physical asset is easier to describe than the life around it. I wanted to ask whose needs give the project its purpose and what the place makes possible for them.

03 / 04

Connecting commercial and human value

For my current interests, the forum offers a reminder to ask who a project is intended to serve.

Investment and development can be discussed through numbers and physical outputs, but the experience of people is another part of the picture I want to understand.

The connection

That became a question I wanted to follow into my writing.

Read the deeper context+

How do the commercial aims of a development connect to the people who use it? What would make the project valuable in everyday life? The journal essay gives that thought more room, because it has relevance well beyond a single event.

04 / 04

A wider learning context

This event sits alongside finance, technology, and governance experiences in my portfolio.

Together, they encourage me to look beyond the most visible element of a subject and consider the wider organisation and purpose around it.

The connection

I want to carry that human perspective into future reading about businesses and investment.

Read the deeper context+

A proposal has numbers and physical outputs, but it also has an intended purpose. Asking who benefits, and how, helps me understand the story behind a project rather than treating the visible result as the whole explanation.

My original reflection

I first shared my thoughts in the post linked below. Here, I have given the ideas more room and connected them to the questions I want to explore next.
